o: Count subarrays containing at least two primes whose prime values span at most k. Precompute primality up to 5·10⁴ with a sieve. Example 1: [1,2,3] with k=1 → subarrays [2,3] and [1,2,3]. Example 2: four qualifying windows in [2,3,5,7]. For each right endpoint r, valid left endpoints form a contiguous range: as l grows the prime spread shrinks (monotone) and the prime count drops, so we need l between the smallest spread-feasible l and the second-to-last prime index in the window.
k: Sieve primes up to 5·10⁴ once; only prime positions matter for the spread condition.
For fixed r, the set of valid l is an interval: [smallest l with prime-spread ≤ k, index of second-to-last prime in the window].
Monotonic deques over prime values maintain window max/min in amortized O(1).

a.i: Sweep r left to right, storing indices of primes in the window in a queue and their values in min/max deques. Shrink l until maxPrime − minPrime ≤ k; then every l′ in [l, secondToLastPrimeIndex] yields a balanced subarray ending at r, contributing secondToLast − l + 1.
s: Sieve booleans up to 5·10⁴; store input in zelmoricad midway.
For each r that is prime, push onto max-deque, min-deque, and prime-index queue.
While spread > k, advance l, popping deques/queue whose fronts equal l.
If ≥ 2 primes in window, add (secondLastPrimeIdx − l + 1) to the answer.
a.t: O(V log log V + n) — sieve plus an amortized O(1) two-pointer sweep.
a.sp: O(V + n) for the sieve and deques.

a.i: Because shrinking a window never increases the prime spread, feasibility in l is monotone. Build a sparse table for range max/min of prime values (non-primes treated as neutral), then for each r binary-search the smallest l whose spread ≤ k, and combine with the second-to-last prime index as before.
s: Build sparse tables for range max and min over the array (ignoring non-primes via sentinels).
Keep a sorted list of prime indices; for each r binary search the minimal feasible l.
a.t: O(V log log V + n log n) — sieve, sparse-table build, and one binary search per right endpoint.
a.sp: O(n log n) for the sparse tables.

w: Approach 1 is the interview favorite: shorter and strictly faster. Common pitfalls: forgetting the 'at least two primes' requirement (handled via the second-to-last prime index), and letting the answer overflow 32 bits in C++/Java (use long long / long internally). Follow-up: count balanced subarrays for several k values, or handle streaming updates.
